idiom_name: Hash per scope plus a parent link (array of open scopes), define/lookup methods
implementation_notes: Ruby's Hash plus a parent reference is the whole structure: a Scope class holding an entry hash and a parent, define rejecting a name already present in the same hash and lookup walking outward - Ruby's own parser tracks local-variable tables per scope, and blocks, def, class and module establish the nesting the table must mirror. What replaces the classic structure is Hash plus Ruby's block scoping (blocks and lambdas close over the surrounding scope, so the resolver's scope stack is a small array pushed on entry and popped on exit), and Struct or Data cover entry types without a class hierarchy. Keep this hand-rolled form for interpreters and DSL tooling; for Ruby source itself, Ripper and Prism expose the syntax tree (Ripper.sexp, Ripper.lex) and MRI's RubyVM::AbstractSyntaxTree the AST, but none of them publishes a resolution or scope API, so name analysis is derived from the tree.
code_sketch:
Scope = Struct.new(:parent, :symbols) do
  def define(name, sym)                       # duplicate in this scope -> false
    return false if symbols.key?(name)
    symbols[name] = sym
  end
  def lookup(name)                            # innermost outward
    scope = self
    scope = scope.parent until scope.nil? || scope.symbols.key?(name)
    scope&.symbols&.fetch(name, nil)
  end
end
pitfalls: Hash lookups test truthiness badly: a symbol whose value is nil or false looks absent to if sym, so always probe with key? (and give scope hashes no default block).

Ruby's scoping is not uniformly lexical for def: method bodies do not close over surrounding locals while blocks and lambdas do, so a resolver that treats def like a lambda resolves outer locals the language would not.
A mutable Hash key damages the hash index (the key's hash changes), so intern identifier strings or freeze them and keep symbol keys stable.
